name: Interview market making, set 4
description: Market-making questions interviewers ask: card and dice fair values, informed flow, limits, hedges, arbitrage, edge and calibration. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: An ace counts 1, a number card its number, a jack 11, a queen 12 and a king 13. From one shuffled deck, five cards lie face up: king, queen, 9, 4 and ace. A contract pays the rank of the next card dealt.
items.question: What is the contract's fair value? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the points shown out of the deck and average what is left.

byKey.full-deck: You ignored the five cards shown. They take 39 points out of the deck.
byKey.over-52: You divided by 52. Only 47 cards are left to deal.
byKey.seen-mean: You averaged the cards shown. The next card comes from the 47 that are left.

explain.text: The full deck holds 4 × 91 = 364 points. The five cards shown hold 13 + 12 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 39. The 47 left average (364 − 39)/47 = 325/47 ≈ 6.91.

items.prose: The interviewer rolls a fair four-sided die and a fair eight-sided die. "Make me a market on the product of the two faces."
items.question: What fair value do you centre your market on?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the independence of the two dice.

byKey.range-mid: You took the middle of 1 and 32. Most products are small, so the mean sits lower.
byKey.added: You added the two means. The contract pays the product.

explain.text: The dice are independent, so the mean of the product is the product of the means. That is 2.5 × 4.5 = 11.25. Centre on 11.25 and widen for the long tail up to 32.

items.prose: You quote 98 at 102 around a fair value of 100. A buyer lifts your offer at 102. Later you learn they knew the true value was 111. Each uninformed trade earns you half the width, 2, on average.
items.question: What is the fewest uninformed trades that win back the loss?

widget.accept: 5: the loss is 9, and 4 trades earn only 8.
widget.label: Trades

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the loss on the informed trade, then divide by what one uninformed trade earns.

byKey.fraction: You stopped at 4.5. Trades come whole, and 4 trades earn only 8.
byKey.from-fair: You measured the loss from fair 100. You sold at 102, so you lost 9, not 11.
byKey.full-width: You counted the full width, 4, per trade. One trade earns half the width.

explain.text: You sold at 102 something worth 111, so you lost 111 − 102 = 9. Each uninformed trade earns 2 on average. You need 9/2 = 4.5, so 5 whole trades.

items.prose: You are long 9 lots, and your limit is 10 lots either way. At the same moment, one customer wants to sell you 3 lots. Another wants to buy 4 lots from you.
items.question: How do you fill them?

options.text: Sell 4 to the buyer first, then buy 3 from the seller: you go 9, 5, 8
Buy 3 from the seller first, then sell 4: the net is −1 either way
options.why: You looked only at the net. Buying first takes you to 12, over the limit, before the sale.

options.text: Refuse both, since you are close to the limit
options.why: You treated every trade as risk. The sale moves you away from the limit, and then the purchase fits.

options.text: Fill only the seller, since buying at your bid is your edge
options.why: Buying 3 lots alone takes you to 12, two over the limit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check your position after each fill, not only at the end.

explain.text: The limit holds after every trade, not only at the end. Selling first takes you to 5, then buying 3 gives 8, inside 10. Buying first would reach 12.

items.prose: You are long 40 call contracts, each on 100 shares. Each call has a delta of 0.35.
items.question: How many shares do you sell to hedge?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shares the calls cover, then scale by the delta.

byKey.per-share: You left out the 100 shares in each contract.
byKey.no-delta: You hedged every share as if the delta were 1. Each call moves only 0.35 per share.
byKey.one-minus: You used 1 − 0.35. The delta is 0.35, so hedge 0.35 of each share.

explain.text: The calls cover 40 × 100 = 4,000 shares. Each moves 0.35 for each £1 move in the share. So you sell 0.35 × 4,000 = 1,400 shares.

items.prose: Three contracts each pay £100 if their outcome happens, and exactly one outcome will. A dealer quotes A at 28 to 30, B at 33 to 35 and C at 30 to 32.
items.question: Which trade locks in a sure profit?

options.text: Buy one of each at the offers: pay £97, collect £100
Sell one of each at the bids: collect £91
options.why: You sold all three. One of them always pays out £100, so this loses £9.

options.text: Buy only A, the cheapest, at 30
options.why: One contract alone is a bet, not an arbitrage. A pays only if its own outcome happens.

options.text: Buy one of each at the bids: pay £91 for £100
options.why: You bought at the bids. You buy at the dealer's offers and sell at the bids.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a set of contracts that pays the same on every outcome.

explain.text: One of the three always pays £100, so a set of all three is worth exactly £100. The offers add to 30 + 35 + 32 = £97. Buying the set locks in 100 − 97 = £3.

items.prose: A game costs £5. You roll a fair die and are paid the square of the face less 10, in pounds. A negative amount pays nothing, so a 4 pays £6 and a 3 pays nothing.
items.question: What is your edge per game, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the payout of each face, average them, then take off the cost.

byKey.negatives: You let the low faces pay negative amounts. Faces 1, 2 and 3 pay nothing, not −9, −6 and −1.
byKey.square-mean: You squared the average face. Average the payouts of the six faces instead.
byKey.no-cost: You left out the £5 the game costs.

explain.text: Only 4, 5 and 6 pay: £6, £15 and £26. The average payout is (6 + 15 + 26)/6 = 47/6 ≈ £7.83. Less the £5 cost, the edge is 17/6 ≈ £2.83 a game.

items.prose: Over a month you gave 60 ranges, each stated at 90% confidence. Only 45 of them held the true value.
items.question: What do you conclude, and what do you change?

options.text: You are overconfident: 75% held, so widen your ranges
You are underconfident: 75% held, so narrow your ranges
options.why: You read the misses the wrong way. Too few ranges held, so they are too narrow.

options.text: You are well calibrated: 45 hits is within luck of 54
options.why: You expected wide luck. With 60 ranges at 90% the hits vary by about 2.3, so 45 is nearly 4 of those short.

options.text: Your centres are off: move them, but keep the widths
options.why: You blamed the centres. They matter, but too few hits says the ranges are too narrow, so widen them first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the share that held with the 90% you claimed.

explain.text: Stated at 90%, 60 ranges should hold about 54 times. 45 is 75%, and true 90% ranges give 45 or fewer only about 0.07% of the time. Widen each range until about nine in ten hold.
